title: Keys and secrets
standfirst: Three different things are called “secrets”: a value in an environment variable, a file on disk, and a placeholder that a proxy swaps for the real key. Only the third keeps the key away from the agent.
idea: An agent runs as a process inside the machine, usually with root or sudo. Anything in its environment or on its disk is something it can print, copy into a message, or send to a host an attacker controls. Agent 37 says this plainly: anything in an instance's environment, the agent can read and repeat back.

The stronger design keeps the real value outside the machine. The sandbox gets a placeholder that looks like a key but is worthless on its own; an egress proxy recognises it on an outbound request and substitutes the real value, but only for the hosts you named.

The details decide how much it protects you. Which headers are rewritten, whether URLs and bodies are covered, whether non-HTTP protocols work, and whether the machine can bypass the proxy by not using it.

splits.heading: Placeholder plus proxy
body: Runtime, boxd, Blaxel, Vercel, E2B and Sprites all describe some version of this. Runtime rewrites seven named headers and never URLs. Vercel says the secrets never enter the sandbox. Sprites stores the credential in the organisation and routes calls through its gateway. E2B injects the real value into matching HTTPS requests outside the VM.
The limits differ. InstaBox's proxy handles HTTPS on port 443 only, with no body or URL substitution and no WebSocket upgrades. Blaxel's proxy is in public preview.

splits.heading: Environment variables are still the default
body: Agent 37 has no general secret manager: your keys go in environment variables the agent can read, plus a per-instance token for its four managed services. Sandboxer's environments inject variables, secret files and repositories into the VM. Lizard's create-time envs reach every command. Morph has a template-integrated secret manager and scoped agent tokens, but proxy semantics are not published.
That is fine when the agent is yours. It is not fine when the agent browses untrusted pages and can be talked into exfiltrating what it can see.

splits.heading: Where secrets leak without an attack
body: The common leak is a snapshot. InstaBox's home is /data/home, so a snapshot includes saved GitHub, Claude, Codex, git and SSH logins, and every machine built from it inherits them. Lizard's snapshot copies a volume's files and shares them with anyone who can restore it. boxd wipes in-VM agent logins when a machine is shared.
The second leak is a shell that never loads the secret. InstaBox's secrets arrive through a profile script, so systemd units and non-login shells never see them.

watchFor: Whether the agent can read the key or only use it.
Which hosts the key can be sent to, and what happens for any other host.
Whether the proxy covers headers only, or also URLs and bodies.
Whether secrets end up in snapshots and forks.
Whether a process that skips the login shell still sees the secret.

rows.scenario: The key is an environment variable, so it prints with everything else; the per-instance token only covers four managed services.
rows.note: Instances boot with a per-instance token for four managed services, but there is no general secret manager: your own keys go in environment variables the agent can read.

source.quote: Anything in an instance's environment, the agent can read and repeat back.

rows.scenario: The proxy injects headers, body fields and secrets server-side, so the machine holds nothing to print — in public preview.
rows.note: The proxy intercepts outbound HTTPS and injects headers, body fields and secrets server-side, but the feature is in public preview and tools that ignore proxy variables can bypass filtering.

source.quote: The Blaxel proxy intercepts outbound HTTPS requests from the sandbox and injects headers, body fields, and secrets server-side.

rows.scenario: Sandboxes hold placeholder model keys, and a safe-for-third-parties switch withholds everything of yours.
rows.note: Environment variables and secret files, a safe-for-third-parties switch that withholds everything of yours, and an AI credentials proxy so sandboxes hold placeholder model keys.

source.quote: A placeholder is worthless outside boat. It does not contain the real key.

rows.scenario: The machine holds an opaque bxds_ string, and the proxy swaps in the real key only for that host.
rows.note: Sealed secrets injected at boot, and secrets bound to a host where the machine holds an opaque `bxds_` string and the proxy swaps in the real key for that host only.

source.quote: Inside the machine `STRIPE_KEY` is an opaque string starting with `bxds_`.

rows.scenario: The Worker holds the key and adds it after the request leaves the sandbox, so the agent prints nothing useful — unless the key was put in the sandbox.
rows.note: The credential stays in the Worker and is added by an outbound handler after the request leaves. Add it only to HTTPS. Once a value is in the sandbox, all code there can read it and send it anywhere.

source.quote: A Container can send its request without the credential, and an outbound handler in your Worker adds the credential after the request leaves the sandbox.

rows.scenario: The agent prints a dtn_secret placeholder; the real key is added to HTTPS headers only, so a JSON-body or query-string call cannot authenticate.
rows.note: A `dtn_secret_…` placeholder is swapped by an outbound proxy in HTTPS request headers only; bodies and query strings fail. A secret without an allowlist is substituted for every host.

source.quote: The proxy substitutes placeholders in HTTPS request headers only.

rows.scenario: The real value is injected outside the sandbox, but the destination receives it and could echo it back in its response.
rows.note: An egress proxy injects the real value into matching outbound HTTPS requests outside the sandbox. The destination receives the value and could expose it in its response.

source.quote: The egress proxy injects the real value into matching outbound HTTPS requests outside the sandbox.

rows.scenario: The sandbox sees an ibsec_ placeholder; the real value is added only to HTTPS headers on port 443 to named hosts.
rows.note: Org Secrets in proxy mode: the sandbox sees an `ibsec_` placeholder and the real value is added only to HTTPS headers on port 443 to named hosts. Env mode exposes the value.

source.quote: Only in HTTPS request headers (port 443) to the Secret's `hosts`, where the outbound proxy swaps it in.

rows.scenario: Secrets are create-time environment variables that reach every command, so the agent prints the real value.
rows.note: Secrets are create-time environment variables that reach every command, plus a scoped CLI key per sandbox that dies with it. No proxy and no host binding.

rows.scenario: By default the key is an environment variable the agent can print; the beta outbound policy keeps it outside the sandbox instead.
rows.note: Secrets arrive as environment variables by default. A beta Outbound Policy injects credentials into outbound HTTPS outside the sandbox and is immutable per configuration. OIDC identity tokens are available.

source.quote: This replacement happens outside the Sandbox so the secret never appears in the Sandbox's environment.

rows.scenario: A template-integrated secret manager and scoped agent tokens exist, but whether a proxy keeps values out of the VM is not published.
rows.note: Devbox templates integrate a secrets manager, and agent tokens carry scoped secret permissions. Whether a proxy keeps values out of the VM is not published.

source.quote: Every devbox is created from a template that integrates with our secrets manager

rows.scenario: The machine sees a placeholder, and OIDC tokens let AWS or GCP trust the sandbox without a stored key.
rows.note: The machine sees a placeholder, and the value is added only to HTTPS requests to the hosts you name. OIDC tokens let AWS or GCP trust a sandbox without a stored key.

source.quote: The machine sees a placeholder. The value is added only to HTTPS requests to the hosts you name.

rows.scenario: Environments inject variables and secret files into the VM, with no broker or short-lived credential exchange.
rows.note: An environment injects variables, secret files and repositories into the VM, and removing a secret deletes it from disk. There is no broker or short-lived credential exchange.

source.quote: Removing a secret from an environment and upgrading **deletes** it from the sandboxes' disks

rows.scenario: Connectors keep the credential in the organisation and route calls through the gateway, so the Sprite never sees it.
rows.note: Connectors store the credential in the organisation and route API calls through the Sprites gateway, so the Sprite never sees the token. A connector with no policy refuses every Sprite.

source.quote: Connectors solve this by storing the credential once, in your organization, and routing API calls through the Sprites gateway. Sprites never see the token.

rows.scenario: Credentials are brokered into egressing traffic, so the value never enters the sandbox and code inside cannot exfiltrate it.
rows.note: Credentials brokering injects credentials into egressing traffic, so secrets never enter the sandbox and code inside cannot exfiltrate them.

source.quote: Credentials brokering injects credentials into egressing traffic. The secrets never enter the sandbox

rows.scenario: The agent can read every credential: keys arrive as command or PTY environment variables, with no proxy, placeholder or per-host scoping.
rows.note: Environment variables are scoped to one command or one PTY session and merged into that process's environment. No secrets manager, placeholder substitution or egress-proxy injection is documented for sandboxes, so a key the agent needs is a key the agent can print. The orchestration product has its own Secrets page, which does not cover sandboxes.

source.quote: Use command-scoped env when values should not persist across all sandbox processes.

rows.scenario: The agent reads whatever is in its environment or on disk; a Droplet has no secret store to keep keys out of reach.
rows.note: API tokens have granular custom scopes. A Droplet has no secret manager: keys go in cloud-init, files or environment variables. Only Managed Agents stores secrets and injects them at session start, and only Action Gateway brokers credentials so the model never sees them.

source.quote: Most scopes in this table are granular scopes that grant access to a specific resource type and action.

rows.scenario: Whatever key the agent needs is a file or an environment variable on the server, readable by anything running there.
rows.note: There is no vault, no write-only environment store and no request-signing proxy. Cloud-init user data (up to 32 KiB) is the only documented first-run injection and it lives on the disk. API tokens, by contrast, are properly scoped: one project each, read-only or read-write.

source.quote: As an alternative to working directly with our API you may also consider to use:

rows.scenario: The agent pastes its environment into a message because the keys live in the OS environment, not a provider vault.
rows.note: There is no provider secret store, no hidden-secret proxy and no scoped key. API tokens inherit the permissions of the user who created them and can be set to expire, but cannot be limited to one machine or one action.

source.quote: Tokens inherit the permissions of the user who created them and can be set to expire.

scenario.title: The agent pastes its environment into a message
scenario.setup: The agent holds a key for a paid search API. A page it is reading tells it to print its environment for debugging, and it copies the output into a chat message that leaves the machine.

beats.what: You add the key. Whether it lands in the environment or in a proxy decides everything that follows.
The agent prints what it can see. A placeholder is worthless; a real key is now in a transcript.
The agent calls the API anyway. A proxy substitutes the value on the way out, but only for the hosts you named.

scenario.turn: The dividing line is whether the value exists inside the machine. A proxy that covers headers only is narrower than one that covers bodies, and a snapshot can carry the secret even when the proxy is perfect.

questions: Can a process inside the machine read the real value, or only a placeholder?
Which hosts is the value sent to, and what happens to a request to any other host?
Does the proxy cover headers only, or also URLs, bodies and WebSocket upgrades?
Do snapshots and forks carry the secret or saved logins, and who can restore them?
Does a systemd unit or a non-login shell see the secret, or only an interactive login?
